purpose: Exact local-PDF locators and paraphrased proof routes supporting CKSD formalization. Source correspondence is distinguished from a completed Lean proof.
page_convention: PDF page numbers are one-based physical pages. A pair denotes an inclusive range; printed_pages records book page labels.
source_policy: Original PDFs remain in the sibling References and ReferencesSuppl directories.
This index stores bibliographic metadata and original paraphrases, not full-book text.
A source proof is used only after its hypotheses, conventions and scope have been compared with the Lean statement.
Source passages, including proof outlines and deferred exercises, are not themselves certified Lean proofs.

text_extraction.cache_location: Temporary files outside the project; PDF filenames and checksums in this index identify the durable source.
text_extraction.scanned_pages: OCR text and mathematical displays should be checked against rendered PDF pages when notation, constants or hypotheses are unclear.

proof_route: For finite outcome spaces, form the compact convex set of stochastic matrices M. If no garbling exists, apply finite-dimensional bilinear minimax/separation to the payoff trace((PM-Q)C).
The decision comparison makes the game value nonpositive. A minimizing matrix M then has every coordinate of PM-Q nonpositive; row sums equal zero, hence PM=Q.

For the current arbitrary measurable X and standard-Borel Y, first pass to dominated likelihood/posterior simplex laws. General measurable randomization then needs a compactness/separation argument or a convex-order martingale coupling followed by conditional disintegration.
assumption_comparison: The cited theorem assumes both experiments have finitely many outcomes; the current Lean theorem assumes only finite parameter type. The matrix theorem alone does not prove the Lean statement.
The finite parameter family is dominated by the finite sum of its laws. No standard-Borel hypothesis on X should be introduced; Y is already nonempty standard Borel.
A posterior-prior construction must handle empty parameter type separately before normalizing a uniform prior.
lean_obligations: General dominated-experiment randomization/separation, beyond the finite stochastic-matrix game.
Composition of a proposed garbling kernel with finite-action rules and the corresponding risk identity.
Posterior-simplex convex-order coupling and measurable disintegration if following that route.

citations.locator: Theorem 7.10, joint subsequence and conditional-law representation; Lemma 7.11
Theorem 9.3 and Theorem 9.4, general experiment representation and LAN limit experiments
Theorem 8.3, estimator representation consequence

proof_route: Use convergence of T_n and the central sequence under parameter zero to extract one joint limiting law rho for (Delta_n,T_n).

For each fixed h, combine the same joint subsequence with the LAN expansion and Le Cam's third lemma. This gives L_h(B)=integral 1_B(s) exp(inner(h,z)-inner(h,Ih)/2) d rho(z,s). No uncountable diagonal subsequence is needed: the joint subsequence is fixed at parameter zero, and each h is treated afterward.
Disintegrate rho with respect to its Gaussian observation marginal. Tilting rho only in the observation coordinate preserves this single conditional kernel.
Identify the tilted Gaussian marginal as N(Ih,I), then pull the kernel back along x maps to I*x to obtain the requested N(h,I inverse) input experiment.
assumption_comparison: Theorem 7.10 is stated for iid QMD experiments and Euclidean-valued statistics. The current Lean theorem starts directly from LAN and permits nonempty Polish Borel statistic spaces. The proof uses only LAN, tightness and standard-Borel disintegration, so those are legitimate extensions requiring explicit Lean adapters.
Theorem 9.3 assumes a dominated limit experiment; the nonsingular Gaussian shift satisfies this. The book omits its general proof, but gives the needed LAN special-case proof in Theorem 7.10.
No tightness assumption on T_n must be added: convergence under h=0 already supplies tightness in this target.

The newly proved kernel bridge requires only a finite joint base measure, measurable nonnegative extended densities and a nonempty standard-Borel output space. It does not require a measurable parameter space or an inverse coordinate map.
lean_obligations: Joint tightness and subsequence extraction for statistic/central-sequence laws on Polish product spaces.
General measurable-output Le Cam third-lemma transfer for the joint subsequence. Existing CKSD log-likelihood transfer is real-valued, so its interface needs a product/Polish-output form.
Multivariate Gaussian exponential-density tilt and the covariance/linear-map identity involving I and I inverse.
Connect those inputs to the proved tilted-event-probability common-kernel constructor.

citations.locator: Proposition 8.4, equivariant-in-law Gaussian estimator convolution; Bayesian proof
Theorem 8.8, convolution theorem

proof_route: First prove the representation theorem. Regularity makes its randomized Gaussian-limit estimator equivariant in law.
Introduce a Gaussian prior on the shift and decompose the error into an independent Gaussian posterior residual and a remainder. Send the prior covariance to infinity.

The error law remains L; divide characteristic functions by the positive Gaussian factor, use a continuity/existence theorem to obtain a limiting remainder law, and identify convolution by characteristic-function uniqueness.
assumption_comparison: The source QMD/iid assumptions are used to reach the representation theorem; the subsequent Gaussian equivariance proposition is a finite-sample Gaussian statement matching the needed LAN conclusion.
A finite covariance of L is not needed for convolution existence. It is needed only for the separate covariance-bound conclusion in the source, which is absent from the Lean theorem.
Do not impose pointwise equivariance on the kernel: regularity gives equivariance in law only.
lean_obligations: Complete 102.15 or give an equivalent direct joint-limit argument.
Prove the Gaussian equivariant-in-law convolution proposition for Markov kernels.
Gaussian-prior posterior/residual independence, covariance convergence, tightness or Levy continuity to produce a remainder measure, and characteristic-function convolution identification.

citations.locator: Lemma 8.5 and Proposition 8.6, Gaussian concentration/minimax
Theorem 8.11 and displayed proof, including tightness restriction and compactification footnote

proof_route: Choose subsequences realizing minimax liminf bounds on successively larger finite rational local-parameter sets.
Extract a joint estimator/score limit, transfer it to a randomized estimator in the Gaussian experiment, and use portmanteau for nonnegative lower-semicontinuous loss.
Apply the Gaussian minimax risk bound; lower semicontinuity extends the rational-parameter supremum to all local parameters.
For unrestricted estimator sequences, add a compactification device before joint-limit extraction, rather than assuming tightness.
assumption_comparison: Theorem 8.11 states the full minimax result but its supplied proof explicitly assumes tightness of the scaled estimator at the base parameter and lower-semicontinuity of loss. Its footnote refers elsewhere for the compactification argument removing tightness.
The current Lean theorem already assumes lower-semicontinuous symmetric quasiconvex ENNReal loss, but does not assume estimator tightness. The displayed proof alone is therefore insufficient.

The source uses a supremum over finite parameter subsets; the Lean bound uses expanding balls, which dominate every finite subset. Extended nonnegative losses require truncation/monotone convergence around the bounded-loss argument.
Anderson's Gaussian concentration inequality is a separate missing prerequisite; it must not be treated as an immediate consequence of covariance comparison.
lean_obligations: Gaussian Anderson inequality for symmetric convex sets, then the associated nonnegative bowl-shaped-loss integral inequality.
Finite-experiment minimax/portmanteau subsequence argument and l.s.c Gaussian-shift risk.
Compactification or another argument valid without base-parameter estimator tightness.

citations.locator: Lemma 25.14, QMD one-dimensional paths and their LAN expansions
Theorem 25.20, convolution, and its finite-dimensional tangent-subspace proof
Lemma 25.23, efficient regularity iff asymptotic linearity
Section 3.3, condition (iii), Theorem 3.3.2 A/B and proof
Proposition 3.3.1, regular asymptotically-linear estimators and efficient influence functions
Section 3.4, Proposition 3.4.1 and Corollary 3.4.1, nuisance projection and inverse-information influence function

proof_route: Use the score family a dot ell + g, with g in the linear nuisance space, to identify the closed tangent linear space. Project ell orthogonally off the nuisance closure and show the inverse efficient-information score is the canonical gradient.

Apply the parametric Gaussian representation/convolution argument on finite-dimensional tangent subspaces. Approximate the efficient influence coordinates in L2 and send the projected covariance matrices to the efficient covariance.

Alternatively, BKRW Theorem 3.3.2 gives an explicit joint characteristic-function factorization: approximate linear combinations of efficient influence coordinates and arbitrary tangent scores by actual submodel scores, then identify an independent remainder.

For the efficiency equivalence, asymptotic linearity implies regularity through QMD local likelihood transfer; necessity follows by jointly representing the efficient influence sample sum and the estimator, whose Gaussian projection residual vanishes at the information bound.
assumption_comparison: The source requires pathwise differentiability and regularity along the tangent paths. The Lean hypotheses encode a linear score family with exact parameter derivative a; the corresponding canonical-gradient identities still need proof.

BKRW condition (iii) is a tangent-richness/approximability assumption on the efficient gradient coordinates. The current score family contains every (a,g) and G is linear, so the needed approximability should be derived from the closure of span(ell)+G, not added as a new hypothesis.
The Lean paths need only QMD at zero. BKRW printedp67/PDF93 explicitly notes that its proof remains valid under differentiability at zero instead of continuous differentiability of submodels.

The current IsRegularAlongPaths definition tests t=1/sqrt(n) for every selected score direction; reduction to all local scalar shifts on a fixed submodel requires an asymptotic equivalence argument for QMD paths with the same scaled score. This must be established explicitly.
The nuisance space is linear, so the source linear-tangent proof applies; the extra cone complications of van der Vaart's broader theorem need not be formalized for this target.
lean_obligations: Mean-zero scores, the canonical-gradient pairing identities, and efficient influence covariance equal to inverse efficient information.
QMD local-product-law equivalence for two selected paths with the same first-order score; finite-dimensional LAN assembly from the indexed one-dimensional paths.
Complete the parametric representation/convolution backbone and then prove closure stability of Gaussian convolution factors.
Joint weak convergence and characteristic-function/independence factorization; efficient regularity to asymptotic linearity.

proof_route: Prove the one-step EVI 2*h*KL(mu_(n+1),pi) <= (1-alpha*h)*W2(mu_n,pi)^2 - W2(mu_(n+1),pi)^2 + 2*beta*d*h^2.

Split one ULA step into deterministic gradient descent and Gaussian heat convolution. The gradient descent energy inequality and Gaussian energy increment are elementary smoothness/coupling estimates. The entropy decrease part is the heat-flow Wasserstein EVI.
Iterate the scalar recurrence to get last-iterate W2 convergence. Telescope over n=N,...,2N-1 and apply convexity of KL to get the mixture-of-laws bound.
Choose universal numerical c,C and h=c*epsilon^2/(beta*d), convert geometric factors to exponentials, and verify the given logarithmic iteration threshold.
assumption_comparison: Exact match to the strongly convex part of Theorem4.3.6: the output is the mixture N^(-1)*sum_{j=N+1}^{2N} mu_j, not the law of an arithmetic average of positions.
The book controls sqrt(KL) by epsilon; the Lean target correctly controls KL by epsilon^2. The W2 normalization is sqrt(alpha)*W2 <= epsilon.
The book assumes finite initial W2 for its coupling proof; the target MemLp id 2 mu0 and strong convexity give this after proving Gibbs has second moment.
The d=0 case is vacuous under 0<epsilon<=sqrt(d); do not divide by d before eliminating it.
lean_obligations: Heat-flow entropy EVI on measures, including singular initial laws; relative entropy/free energy change of reference.
Convexity of KL for a finite mixture with its exact ENNReal normalization.
Finite-moment Gaussian convolution and the discrete EVI; remaining recurrence/iteration arithmetic is comparatively small.

proof_route: Prove existence of the free-energy resolvent by a narrowly lower-semicontinuous direct method with Gaussian entropy lower bounds and second-moment control.

Prove uniqueness using strict convexity of entropy along ordinary mixtures: potential energy is linear and squared Wasserstein distance to a fixed measure is mixture-convex. This argument does not require V to be convex.
Establish the entropy-plus-potential first variation for compactly supported vector-field perturbations, giving the full JKO Euler-Lagrange equation.
Derive finite-horizon moment, entropy and summed squared-increment bounds; construct constant and transport interpolations and prove their fluxes have the same weak limit.

Identify the weak FP equation by testing the discrete Euler-Lagrange relation and passing to the limit. Upgrade subsequences to full convergence using weak-PDE uniqueness, even though uniqueness is not explicitly part of the target conclusion.

For the stated strong space-time L1 convergence, add spatial compactness/Fisher-information or translation estimates and time-translation control. Weak L1 compactness alone does not imply this conclusion.
assumption_comparison: Santambrogio Section 8.3 assumes a compact domain Omega and Lipschitz V. CKSD works on all R^d with V smooth, nonnegative, and norm(gradient V) <= C*(V+1). This is not a direct instance of Proposition 8.10.

On a compact domain entropy is uniformly bounded below; for the allowed CKSD example V=0 on R^d the free energy is unbounded below. Use Gaussian moment compensation and finite-horizon estimates, not Proposition 8.8 with a finite global infimum.

The inspected Santambrogio argument establishes narrow/uniform W2 subsequential convergence and weak L1 through equi-integrability. It does not by itself state the stronger global space-time L1 convergence required by the CKSD theorem.

Villani2009 discusses the discrete JKO proof but refers the full proof to his 2003 volume Section 8.4; Theorem24.2 explicitly assumes much stronger regularity and decay, so it cannot silently justify the present weak-solution theorem.
No counterexample to CKSD was found; the verified mismatch is between the inspected proof scope and the target scope, not a conclusion that the target is false.
lean_obligations: Properness, narrow lower semicontinuity along W2-bounded sequences, Gaussian entropy coercivity and all-time-step resolvent existence for the sum energy.
Mixture strict entropy convexity and mixture Wasserstein squared-cost convexity for uniqueness without geodesic convexity of V.
Entropy first variation under vector-field pushforwards; upstream Euler-Lagrange potential-only theorem does not provide this.
Finite-horizon compactness and flux identification; global L1 space-time compactness; uniqueness of the weak FP equation under the stated growth assumption.

proof_route: After the same weak-FP/semigroup identification, regularize a positive density r and prove d/dt Ent_pi(P_t r) = -integral norm(gradient(P_t r))^2/(P_t r).

Pavliotis writes the spectral/LSI rate as lambda; lambda=1/C here, and inverse temperature is 1. His stated theorem additionally invokes a smooth Bakry-Emery potential; BGL/Chewi supply the more general LSI equivalence actually needed.

CKSD only assumes V is C2 with Lipschitz gradient and its flow is weak. The book differentiations require generator-domain/regularized solutions. Do not add classical-solution hypotheses to the original target to fit those computations.

proof_route: Construct the reversible Langevin Markov semigroup P_t with generator Delta minus gradV dot grad, and prove every CKSD weak probability-valued Fokker-Planck flow is its forward law.

For a density r0 in L2(pi), identify the evolved density with P_t r0 and chiSq with the variance of P_t r0. Gibbs integration by parts gives d/dt Var(P_t r0) = -2*integral norm(gradient(P_t r0))^2. Apply PI and scalar comparison.

For the converse, use bounded smooth mean-zero f and initial density 1+epsilon*f, differentiate the assumed decay at time zero, cancel epsilon squared, then use cutoff/truncation density to reach all tests in the current PI predicate.
If initial chiSq is infinite the bound is automatic because exp(-2*t/C) is strictly positive; isolate this extended-value case before any toReal conversion.
assumption_comparison: The normalization matches exactly: Pavliotis inverse temperature is set to 1, BGL Dirichlet energy is integral norm(gradient)^2, and CKSD covariance 2I gives the same generator. The decay rate is 2/C.

BGL and Chewi quantify over the constructed semigroup, not arbitrary weak solutions. CKSD IsLangevinFlow provides compact-test integral identities only. Representation/uniqueness must be proved rather than silently assumed.

BGL works on the closed Dirichlet-form domain; pinned TauCeti defines PI on C-infinity admissible tests. This is a real Lean domain-extension obligation, not evidence that the mathematical CKSD statement is false.
lean_obligations: Gibbs weighted integration by parts; closed symmetric generator/Dirichlet form or an alternative explicit additive-noise construction.
Weak FP uniqueness and semigroup representation for the globally Lipschitz C1 drift, for arbitrary initial probability laws.
L2 density transport, time differentiability of variance, approximation at t=0, and extension from smooth compact functions to the form domain.
